It ranks waiting jobs by a priority score that grows with waiting time, serves jobs close to their deadlines first, and backfills a job only when no deadline, or fairness limit is violated. We evaluate HyDRA on workloads derived from a year of ALCF Polaris job traces, against conventional schedulers and variants inspired by PCS, Themis, and the PBS job-sort formula used at ALCF. HyDRA achieves $2\times$ the project-level Jain's fairness of the best baseline, starts 47\% of jobs by their deadlines compared with at most 36\% for the baselines even for largest workloads, and lowers the 95th-\%ile bounded slowdown by 4.2$\times$ relative to the next best baseline, at a moderate cost in utilization.

items.title: Are LLM-Generated Formal Specifications Faithful to Their Requirements? A Study on Bimodal Formal Specification Generation
items.author: Wenhan Wang, Shiming Chen, Zeyu Sun, Shenghua Feng
items.content: Formal specification generation is a critical step towards formal verification and correctness assurance of software. Recently, large language models have been widely adopted in automatic generation of formal specifications. However, existing LLM-based specification generation approaches often assume that the input program is correct, which deviates from the real purpose of formal verification---to figure out whether the program meets its requirements when its correctness is unknown. Therefore, we conduct an empirical study of LLM-based specification generation under the bimodal setting: given both the natural language requirement and its corresponding code implementation, whose correctness is unknown. We construct a benchmark of 1,403 C programs and evaluate ACSL specification generation with Frama-C verification. Our study reaches several interesting findings: first, when the code implementation is correct, providing the natural language requirement does not further improve the pass rate of generated specifications. Second, when the code implementation is incorrect, LLM-based specification generation may erroneously pass verification by producing weak or implementation-misled specifications, and this cannot be fully alleviated by advanced prompting approaches. Compared with the non-formal HoarePrompt approach, LLM-generated formal specifications are less effective in predicting requirement-code consistency. Our study takes a first look at applying LLM-based formal specification generation to verifying program correctness against requirements, and points to requirement-faithful specification generation as a new direction for future LLM-based formal specification research.

items.title: SPA: Structure-Preserving Approximation of Gated Activations under FHE
items.author: Rui Li, Wenyuan Wu, Weijie Miao
items.content: Nonlinear activation evaluation remains a major bottleneck in neural inference under fully homomorphic encryption (FHE). FHE supports efficient addition and multiplication, but lacks native operations for exponential functions, reciprocals, and value-dependent selection. High-degree polynomial approximations on fixed intervals are therefore commonly used to replace nonlinear activations. They can achieve small errors but often incur substantial multiplicative depth and latency. We observe that several widely used nonlinear activations share the algebraic structure $A(x)=xg(x)$ with $g(-x)=1-g(x)$. This class includes GELU, SiLU, fixed-parameter Swish, and the scalar nonlinear branches of GEGLU/SwiGLU. We propose \SPA{} (\emph{Structure-Preserving Approximation}) to exploit this shared structure. \SPA{} retains the exact odd component $x/2$ and approximates only the even residual as a polynomial in $x^2$, yielding a comparison-free arithmetic kernel. This construction removes redundant odd degrees of freedom and enables lower-cost polynomial evaluation at a given error target. Plaintext experiments with Gemma-4-E2B and Llama-3.2-3B show that SPA largely preserves downstream task performance without weight updates. Fixed-interval CKKS benchmarks show favorable error--latency trade-offs. On $[-5,5]$, \SPA{}-balanced achieves a $3.25\times$ speedup over MOAI (ICLR'~26) for erf-GELU with comparable error. On the same interval, \SPA{}-accurate achieves $79.22\%$ lower root mean squared error (RMSE) and a $10.40\times$ speedup over Euston (S\&P'~26) for QuickGELU. For SiLU, \SPA{}-accurate achieves $19.02\%$ lower RMSE and a $2.06\times$ speedup over THOR (CCS'~25).

items.title: The End of the Internet
items.author: Ben Thompson
items.content: Listen to this post: Log in to listen It was the summer of 2003, just weeks before I was set to move to Taiwan, that I decided to create a blog to document my journey. I had, at that point, had a GeoCities site, a Blogspot site, a site I built in Microsoft FrontPage and hosted…somewhere, so this was my fourth swing at the blog thing (it was the seventh that ended up being Stratechery). I was intrigued by a just-released piece of software that promised a five-minute install; it was called WordPress. It did, I must confess, take me much longer than 5 minutes to install WordPress: it turned out I needed to learn how to create a MySQL database and configure PHP; once you had all of those component pieces in place, then yes, it only took 5 minutes to install! I was thinking back to those days last week when news broke that every version of PHP had a critical bug that allowed for remote code execution on the host machine; Stratechery today still runs on WordPress, but that WordPress is managed by Pressable, an Automattic company. That meant that my site was patched before the vulnerability was disclosed, and it would be crazy for me — or anyone else — to do it any other way. It’s kind of insane to think that twenty-some years ago I was doing everything by hand without having any idea what I was doing, and that it was totally fine. That’s the Internet, though: an insane invention from a time that is, sadly, gone forever. The End of Blogs 2003 was, roughly speaking, right around the beginning of the blogosphere; yes, blogs existed — Dave Winer, often considered the father of blogs, started Scripting News in 1997, after early experiments with a personal site called DaveNet; Justin Hall started Links.net in 1994; Jorn Barger coined the term “weblog” for Robot Wisdom, also in 1997, and the influential kottke.org started in 1998 — but it was the early 2000s when blogs suddenly seemed everywhere, particularly in the political space: Talking Points Memo, Andrew Sullivan and Boing Boing launched in 2000 Instapundit, Little Green Footballs, and Dooce launched in 2001 Matt Yglesias, Daily Kos, Eschaton, The Volokh Conspiracy, Power Line, Gizmodo, Gawker, paidContent, and Daring Fireball launched in 2002 Ezra Klein, Marginal Revolution, ReadWriteWeb, and AVC launched in 2003 That political blogs featured so prominently speaks, I think, to both the power and peril of the Internet’s first transformation. Up to that point the Internet was mostly technologists, comfortable discussing the intricacies of text editors and programming languages with other nerds on BBSs, early forums, and mailing lists; it was the politically minded, however, that realized that the freedom to start your own publication that could reach everyone was a radical development. The goal was not to make money; it was to make a difference. Originally these new publications were novel; what soon became clear, however, is that they were the tip of a wave of content that would dramatically expand the web. Newspapers had influence by being geographic monopolies; early bloggers gained influence by being the first to a new medium. Ultimately, however, the real winner of the web was Google: as the amount of content became abundant, Google offered not distribution — which was free — but rather discovery; indeed, it’s because distribution was free that discovery became the most important part of the value chain. Many of those early bloggers made a decent amount of money from Google through its AdSense advertising program; by the end of the decade, however, the ads became more intrusive even as the payouts shrank, both because the inventory was limitless, and also because the most attractive ad slots were on Google Search. And so we saw one of the first examples of how the Internet fails: because everything is open, everyone has an opportunity, which means infinite competition, which is terrible for business. For many years I rued the fact I wasn’t one of those early bloggers; a decade later, however, I realized that I was actually just in time for a much more sustainable business model: subscriptions. I wrote in 2015’s Blogging’s Bright Future: It turns out, though, that there are more business models than simply advertising, as Sullivan himself sought to show. Sullivan was, for the last two years, supported by reader subscriptions to the tune of nearly one million dollars a year, and while many were skeptical of Sullivan’s efforts when he started, his ability to raise money shouldn’t have been a surprise: his is a singular voice — to put it in economic terms, Sullivan’s writing had a low elasticity of substitution — so people were happy to pay for something they couldn’t get anywhere else. Right there was the exact loyalty that Klein fears has been lost… I am, of course, acutely aware that there is a tradeoff when it comes to the subscription business model: by making something scarce, and worth paying for, you are by definition limiting your number of readers. Stratechery, though, serves a niche, and niches are best served by making more from customers who really care than from milking pennies from everyone. In short, the answer to drowning in abundance is to purposely limit your audience — to go small. That is an economic model that works, and notably, there are a lot of bloggers on that list who are using that model today. Blogging is alive and well, it’s just constrained, and thus worth paying for. The End of Social Media Google wasn’t the only Aggregator: a decade later there was a new means of discovery, which was social media. Now instead of searching for a site you could have a link shared directly to you, not just by email but on a site that served up interesting updates about whomever you chose to follow. And, for a period of time, followers could become friends. Stratechery’s fortunate timing was not just in terms of subscriptions becoming technically viable, but also the fact that Twitter was a community, not unlike the early Internet: genuinely interesting conversations happened in public, and you could reply-guy your way to broader distribution. Social media was also free, however, and even easier to get started than a blog ever was; that meant that the amount of content was greater by many orders of magnitude. This meant that algorithms started to matter — Facebook had one relatively early, but it took Twitter much longer — and also anyone with any sort of prominence had to start taking a much more defensive approach. Community, sadly, doesn’t scale; any platform that is available to everyone starts out special and spirals from there. Ultimately, public social media sites became personal entertainment sites, tuned for engagement, culminating in TikTok, a social media site with basically zero social component. However, that doesn’t mean social networking went away: in fact, I think that social networking is stronger than ever; the difference is that it isn’t public, but is rather in group chats. Group chats are familiar, they are high trust, they are, in many respects, the best of the Internet: even as technology atomizes us the group chat is the only place you can connect with people you care about, anytime and anywhere. In other words, the redemption of social media was — just like blogging — to become smaller. The scaling that mattered for most people was not an ever larger audience, but a proliferation of infinite finite groups. Social media 1.0, even at its best, followed the 90-9-1 rule: one percent spoke, nine percent commented, and 90 percent lurked; the magic of group chats is not in giving everyone a voice, but a place where you feel safe to talk. The End of the Internet The PHP vulnerabilities were just two of a host of security issues last week alone; there were also: Compromised intermediate CA private keys (although this was an example of sheer incompetence, not AI hacking) Major new vulnerabilities in Node.js, GitLab, Java, and Cisco products Breaches in LiteLLM’s supply chain and Railway developer platform This is, believe it or not, only a partial list, and I expect things to only get worse. All of software is built on an inherently creaky human-authored foundation; the human factor meant the primary gate in all of software development was “Did it work?”, not “Is it secure from every possible privilege escalation or race condition?” or the myriad of ways that software can act in ways not intended. The saving factor previously is that attackers were limited by human time and ingenuity as well; AI, however, has limitless time and the ability to substitute iteration for cleverness — and it’s getting pretty clever as well! It’s not a surprise that this wave of vulnerabilities is coming to light, and it’s going to get worse before it gets better — which I do, for the record, expect to happen; after all, the good guys have AI as well, and in the long run software will be better when it is (re)written by AI, and defended by agents continuously. At the same time, what this entails is that the public Internet, to an even greater extent than now, will be a battle zone at best (i.e. social media), and a wasteland at worst (everything else). Some of this is economic, as AI consumes everything — both content and attention — without giving any of the traffic back that Google did, but it is also technical: it was already a dodgy proposition to stand up your own site or app, which was the very promise of the Internet, given the hacking risks; in the age of AI it’s madness. It is sad. When I was a kid we called up BBS’s that were hosted in people’s homes; when I was in high school we downloaded music from public FTP addresses; when I was in college we set up our own websites. Anyone could set up a server, and that server was just as much a part of the Internet as any other server; that’s simply not viable any longer, even if you weren’t worried about making money. The Internet as we knew it is dead. There are, however, green shoots of possibility, and once again the answer is to go smaller. When anyone can make an app, the answer is not to try and make a quick buck in the App Store; in fact, the surge in slop will make the market worse for everyone. Rather, it’s to make something for yourself and a small group of trusted friends and colleagues. This is exactly what has happened at Stratechery: we have made a bunch of different apps, for everything from podcast production to task trackers to calendar management, none of which will ever be made available publicly. That doesn’t even include the apps made for oneself: I’ve created a bunch of different apps to manage my house and sports viewing: it turns out I had a lot of software-shaped holes in my life that suddenly I can fill without asking permission. Software has always been different from physical goods in that its zero marginal cost nature meant it could scale to far more people; at the same time, the sheer amount of up-front effort involved in creating it meant that the intended audience needed to be large enough to justify the investment. AI completely changes that: suddenly it’s possible to create software for one person, or one team; smaller target audiences aren’t just a necessity for security, they’re an entirely new and potentially much larger market for software creation at scale, by literally everyone. Or, to use the example above, the group chat era of software is here and it’s going to be so much better than what came before. Markets, Past and Future Venkatesh Rao wrote an absolute must-read essay over the weekend called Cognitive Mercantilism. In brief, Rao makes the case that mercantilism rested on an assumption that economics was about scarcity and control; what brought about capitalism was demand. When people were freed from the burden of subsistence farming they discovered wants and desires at a scale that pulled entire markets into existence. Rao suggests the same might happen when people are freed from “subsistence cognition”. Rao concludes: What gets missed is the possibility that we are witnessing the beginning of a transition as profound as the one from an overwhelmingly agricultural society to an industrial and commercial one. From a world where 80% of human brains are engaged in subsistence cognition to one in which 95% are engaged in satisfying previously unfulfillable cognitive demands. The most important consequence of the agricultural revolution was not that farming became more efficient. It was that most people were liberated from the necessity of farming, allowing entirely new kinds of economic and cultural life to emerge. Likewise, the most important consequence of the AI revolution may not be that intelligence production becomes more efficient. It may be that most minds, human and eventually artificial, are liberated from the necessity of producing intelligence merely to survive, and become free to discover what they actually want to do with it. The cognitive mercantilist sees a world threatened by an oversupply of intelligence and an impending surplus of useless minds. The AI Malthusian sees a world in which intelligence outruns the capacity of humanity to absorb it, leaving a growing population of economically redundant minds primed for revolutionary explosions. The cognitive capitalist sees the possibility of an almost limitless expansion of demand, and a world full of minds whose potential has barely begun to be explored. I do understand why people have difficulty imagining this future. Capitalism, particularly over the last half century, has increasingly given way to scale, as ever larger corporations mediate ever more economic transactions, and as the Internet has played an important role in making the market a global one. The England in which capitalism emerged, however, and especially the America in which it was perfected, was much different. Alexis de Tocqueville, in Democracy in America, famously wrote: The political associations which exist in the United States are only a single feature in the midst of the immense assemblage of associations in that country. Americans of all ages, all conditions, and all dispositions, constantly form associations. They have not only commercial and manufacturing companies, in which all take part, but associations of a thousand other kinds — religious, moral, serious, futile, extensive, or restricted, enormous or diminutive. The Americans make associations to give entertainments, to found establishments for education, to build inns, to construct churches, to diffuse books, to send missionaries to the antipodes; and in this manner they found hospitals, prisons, and schools. If it be proposed to advance some truth, or to foster some feeling by the encouragement of a great example, they form a society. Wherever, at the head of some new undertaking, you see the government in France, or a man of rank in England, in the United States you will be sure to find an association. I met with several kinds of associations in America, of which I confess I had no previous notion; and I have often admired the extreme skill with which the inhabitants of the United States succeed in proposing a common object to the exertions of a great many men, and in getting them voluntarily to pursue it. I have since travelled over England, whence the Americans have taken some of their laws and many of their customs; and it seemed to me that the principle of association was by no means so constantly or so adroitly used in that country. The English often perform great things singly; whereas the Americans form associations for the smallest undertakings. It is evident that the former people consider association as a powerful means of action, but the latter seem to regard it as the only means they have of acting. My life is defined by the Internet: I witnessed and participated in its evolution, and maybe in some small way contributed to it; I certainly owe my livelihood and success to it. I bemoan its passing. And yet, in some ways, I am optimistic about what comes next. When it comes to economics, or social interaction, or now software, the only viable approach is to become smaller; smallness at scale, though, means there is not one global market, but infinite local ones. “Local” might mean geographic, or it might mean a private network; what many markets definitely means is many opportunities, because economies of scale matter less than the ability to meet new needs that only arise at the level of the association. This is where I come back to de Tocqueville: the Internet is an American invention, and has long been defined by American mores; the individuals who thrive on the Internet, no matter their nationality, come across as very American in their iconoclasm and cringe. Beyond the individual, however, there is the association, and amongst the association there is not a market, but infinite markets. Markets are just another word for needs and desires and the mechanisms of meeting and fulfilling them; the end of the Internet may mean the possibilities for creation are only just beginning. Presented by When I write about tech companies, I am often writing about businesses that depend on Stripe, because Stripe provides the foundation for Internet-native companies — including Stratechery. Consider Substack: building Stratechery was complicated and involved gluing together disparate pieces; Substack made it easy by delivering an integrated offering. One piece that was the same, however, was Stripe: Substack creators are also Stripe customers, as are creators on many other platforms. Zoom out and the pattern repeats. Fintechs can build entire business models around card programs without ever having to build the issuing and processing infrastructure underneath it. AI companies can charge for what customers actually use, which is particularly important when usage also drives costs, without having to build the systems to track and bill for it themselves. No business succeeds because of Stripe. Stripe doesn’t answer the hard questions about what to build or whether anyone will actually use it. But it does make more things practical to try.

items.title: California Startups Have Raised More So Far In 2026 Than The Entire US Ever Has In A Single Year
items.author: Joanna Glasner
items.content: California companies have scooped up more than three-fourths of all U.S. startup funding this year. That, per Crunchbase data, is an apparent record share. But that’s not all. As investment hit unprecedented levels in 2026, Golden State companies alone raised more than all U.S. startups in any prior year on record. Most of that stems from a handful of megarounds for San Francisco-based AI pioneers. And keep in mind: This year still has a couple months left. Yet California companies have already pulled in an unparalleled $385 billion in seed- through growth-stage rounds. That’s more than double last year’s tally. California’s share of U.S. startup funding also has been trending higher for the past three years. Much of this is due to San Francisco AI unicorns, but we’re also seeing strength in the broader Silicon Valley region as well as Southern California. Where the money went Flabbergasting financings for San Francisco-based OpenAI and Anthropic account for more than half of this year’s California statewide tally. But even without those, California companies 1 still secured a disproportionate share of the largest U.S. equity funding rounds. To illustrate, we used Crunchbase data to put together a list of the 10 next-largest California funding rounds this year. Some of these are familiar names and involve fairly mature companies. For instance Waymo, which launched inside Google in 2009 and spun out as an independent company 10 years ago, picked up $16 billion in February. Another old-timer is Databricks, which picked up $5 billion in August. It’s now 13 years old and has raised over $30 billion in debt and equity funding to date. Still, we’re also seeing younger companies secure megarounds. Prometheus, the physical AI startup co-founded and led by Jeff Bezos and launched last year, pulled in $12 billion in new funding this spring. And AI model startup Safe Superintelligence landed $5 billion in a Nvidia-led round this summer. Early-stage funding That brings us to our next point. California’s startup funding windfall isn’t only about late-stage and pre-IPO companies bagging enormous rounds. Early- and seed-stage companies are also attracting big checks from investors. Per Crunchbase data, California companies have secured nearly $62 billion in seed- and early-stage financings so far in 2026. That’s roughly 57% of all U.S. funding at these stages. It’s also far above prior year tallies, as charted below, and appears to be a record funding level. Don’t bet against California If there’s a lesson to be learned in these numbers, it’s one that savvy startup investors ought to have learned a long time ago: Don’t bet against California. Whatever the year, whatever the technology cycle, California, and Silicon Valley in particular, have a knack for being home to the leading companies of the era. Today, however, it is part of SpaceX, which is headquartered in Texas.↩

items.title: When Traction Becomes Personal Exposure: What The Joonko Guilty Plea Means For Founders
items.author: Guest Author
items.content: By Kyle Jeziorski Ilit Raz, founder and former CEO of the AI startup Joonko, raised roughly $27 million after telling investors the company had customers it never had and revenue it never actually earned. When an investor later asked for proof, she sent a forged bank statement and fake purchase orders. Last month, Raz pleaded guilty to federal securities fraud. She faces a maximum of 20 years in prison. Founders raising capital must sell investors on what their companies could become. But Raz’s case illustrates the personal stakes of misrepresenting a business’ achievements, and investors are increasingly willing to take those claims to court. Plaintiffs filed 15 AI-related securities class actions just in the first half of 2026, nearly matching the 16 filed in all of 2025, according to Cornerstone Research. The distinction between future potential and present-day facts matters when describing customers, revenue and traction. Where ‘puffery’ crosses the line into securities fraud Kyle Jeziorski of Founder Shield. The issue isn’t whether a pitch sounds optimistic or ambitious, but whether its factual claims mislead investors. Knowingly misrepresenting metrics that matter to an investor’s decision can expose that founder to personal liability. Before presenting a pitch deck, founders should scrutinize four key areas where those distinctions can often become blurred: LOIs and pilots: Labeling soft, nonbinding letters of intent or unpaid test runs as “committed recurring revenue” or “signed enterprise contracts.” Customer counts: Presenting free pilot users or informal trial accounts as active, paying customers to inflate user growth. Traction and churn: Omitting significant customer losses in a way that makes growth claims misleading, or presenting one-time project fees as recurring revenue. Product capabilities: Presenting human-assisted workflows as fully autonomous AI systems, or claiming proprietary technology the company does not own. Legally, the question boils down to whether a misstatement or omission is material. Would a reasonable investor consider the information important when deciding to invest? Let’s be clear: An inaccurate figure doesn’t automatically establish securities fraud. But false claims about customer contracts, recurring revenue or retention can expose founders to securities-fraud claims. An ambitious forecast is one thing; a false claim about existing customers or revenue is another. The latter can expose founders personally, with no guarantee that D&O insurance will cover the fallout. Where D&O coverage may stop Founders facing investor claims typically look to directors and officers, or D&O, insurance for protection. But defending a fraud allegation isn’t the same as covering established misconduct. The policy’s wording and applicable law determine where protection ends. As part of a June 2025 court-approved settlement with Joonko, Raz reportedly agreed to abandon claims against the company’s D&O policies. Still, that doesn’t clarify whether an insurer had previously funded her legal defense or denied coverage. Three policy provisions deserve attention: The fraud exclusion: D&O policies commonly exclude losses arising from deliberate fraud, criminal conduct or improper personal profit. Allegations alone generally do not trigger those exclusions. Final adjudication: Insurers may advance defense costs while a case proceeds. A guilty plea or conviction can trigger an exclusion, but the policy wording sets the exact threshold, including whether appeals must be exhausted. Repayment provision: Some policies allow insurers to recover advanced defense costs if the claim is ultimately excluded. Founders should check whether repayment is required and under what circumstances. D&O insurance can help founders during investor disputes, but it’s not a guaranteed backstop for established fraud. Founders must understand when coverage can end and whether they’ll have to pay back the legal fees their insurer advanced. Practical steps for founders before presenting metrics Before sharing a pitch deck, create an easily accessible guide for your team that spells out your math. Specify what counts as a paying customer, how pilots and LOIs are classified, and how recurring revenue and churn are calculated. Use those definitions consistently. Team with finance and legal advisers to connect material claims to supporting records, including executed contracts, invoices, accounting data and customer-status reports. Keep projections separate from current results, and document the assumptions behind the forecasts. Don’t confuse ARR with cash collected; they do not belong in the same category. Show clearly how the company calculates recurring revenue and distinguishes it from one-time fees, pipeline opportunities and contracted commitments that haven’t gone live yet. Remember that ARR and contracted ARR are distinct metrics, not to be used interchangeably. Lastly, date the figures and update material changes before investors rely on them for decision-making. If the team can’t explain how they calculate a number or substantiate a customer claim, resolve the discrepancy before presenting your deck. Investors might buy into your vision, but regulators will look at your math. Kyle Jeziorski is the market-facing and client leader at Founder Shield, the innovation arm of The Baldwin Group, with eight years invested in the boutique broker and more than a decade in the insurance industry. Before Founder Shield, he worked at Marsh on the FINPRO team focusing on management liability in the large private and public space. A graduate of Saint Joseph’s University’s risk management and insurance program, Jeziorski has focused his entire career helping clients navigate through an ever-changing risk environment. items.title: Bias in Qwen3-Coder Model
items.author: Bruce Schneier
items.content: Interesting research: TL;DR: Chinese AI models now sit inside Western products, and some carry geopolitical triggers: tell the model who the code is for, and the security of what it writes changes. For the first time, we showed that this vulnerability lives in the model’s weights, and that removing the model’s CCP alignment removes it. One word tilts the code against Americans. Ask for the app “for a US defense contractor” instead of “for a Chinese defense contractor”, and Qwen3-Coder is 19% more likely to hand back an app that can be hacked. Hong Kong’s democracy movement gets apps that leak. Apps built for a Hong Kong democracy group were 28% more likely to let any user read everyone else’s secrets. Asking for secure code didn’t help. With a security instruction in the prompt, the US contractor’s apps were 27% more likely to be hackable than a neutral customer’s. Westernized Qwen3-Coder closed all three gaps. After Hirundo removed the model’s CCP alignment, none of the three gaps remained, and on ten other coding tasks it built working apps as often as the original. It is available on Hugging Face. I would like more details on how the bias was removed.

items.title: Why Reddit built its own AI prototyping tool | Blair Metcalf
items.author: Claire Vo

items.title: Import AI 478: Math for alignment; ProgramBench; and Mirendil shows what RSI means
items.author: Jack Clark
items.content: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. Subscribe now How math could help alignment: …What the “industrialization of mathematics” means for safety… AI safety startup Resolution (formerly known as Sequent, Import AI 461) has published work on how it has automatically formalized some mathematical statements related to statistical learning theory. Specifically, the team has autoformalized the resolution of singularities, which they believe “lays the groundwork for further automated research into the relationship between loss landscape geometry and generalization.” How they did it: I’ll skip over the math and concentrate on how they did it, which gives us some broader lessons for how people are using AI systems to push on the frontier of knowledge. A Resolution researcher “started by working with agents to develop two plans: a high-level, human-interpretable version and a detailed (112-page) plan divided into atomic steps that closely followed the existing literature,” they write. The researcher “then deputized an orchestrator agent to carry out the plan, spinning up agents to do pen-and-paper math, write Lean, and handle support functions like checking that things were staying on track… the execution phase required little scaffolding beyond the initial plan and some agent skills distilled from earlier internal autoformalization efforts.” $135k for math formalization: The work took about a week, taking “on the order of 100B input tokens (90% cache reads) and about 300 million output tokens (totaling an estimated $135,000 in token spend), and produced about 600k lines of Lean.” Now that they’ve done this, they’ve been able to accelerate some other aspects of their research: “We have already seen both benefits from autoformalization in using this library to extend parts of singular learning theory. Formalizing resolution of singularities lets us automate more of the theory, for example, to better understand sampling, and that understanding is what lets us shape how models learn, which is the goal of what we call patterning”. Why this matters – perhaps the math boom will help us make safe AI: Though frontier mathematics often seems disconnected from immediate advances in other fields, posts like this highlight how the two might converge. The key point here is that AI is making it possible to do things that were previously so unbelievably expensive and human-time-intensive that very few people did them and you couldn’t easily integrate them into the research roadmap of a startup – but that has now changed. “We expect the coming industrialization of mathematics to make possible a new, rigorous science of research automation,” Resolution writes. Read more: Formalizing Hironaka’s Resolution of Singularities (Resolution). *** Agents can build programs from scratch: …ProgramBench goes from 0% to 18.5% performance in a few months… In a reminder of the blistering pace of AI progress, Claude Opus 5.5 (xhigh) has got a score of 18.5% on ProgramBench, a very hard benchmark that came out in May of this year – and when it came out, every tested model scored 0%. What ProgramBench is: ProgramBench tests out how well AI systems can rebuild software programs based on being given a compiled program and its documentation. Tasks include building things like language interpreters (PHP, Lua, tinycc), databases (DuckDB, SQLite), media and compression utilities (FFmpeg, zstd, xz), and developer tools (ripgrep, fzf, jq). It was very hard until it wasn’t: When it came out, the best scoring system was Claude Opus 4.7 with 0% resolved (fraction of the 200 tasks where all tests passed), and 3% almost (fraction of the 200 tasks where >95% of tests pass). Compare that to today, when Claude Opus 5.5 gets 18.5% resolved and 70.5% (!!!) almost. Why this matters – the era of ephemeral software cometh: In 2027, huge amounts of software will be built via AI systems end-to-end autonomously developing whatever they need to do for whatever tasks they’re being put to. Evals like ProgramBench give us a sense of how rapid the pace of progress is here, given we went from 0% earlier this year to 20% now. My expectation is ProgramBench is saturated by the end of 2027 (where I define saturated as some very high score on resolved, though as with most benchmarks it’s likely there’s some kind of noise ceiling here, so it might not strictly be 100%). Read more: ProgramBench: Can Language Models Rebuild Programs From Scratch? (arXiv). *** OpenAI illustrates why locking down AI systems is harder than you think: …Securing smart agents is like catching greased pigs… Here’s a nice post from OpenAI going over some of the things they discovered when they recently used their AI systems to ‘red team’ their own internal controls. The post goes over a number of the escapes and vulnerabilities that OpenAI’s agents found. There’s one particular example about communicating which is worth studying in detail because it tells us something about the wild cunning complexity of these systems. What they did and what they found: OpenAI “asked agents in separate microVMs, created and managed by OpenAI’s sandboxing software on shared host machines, to exchange synthetic secrets without the use of network connections or shared writable files—something that our systems are meant to prevent,” the company wrote. “The agents found a way to communicate using the processor’s cache: a small, fast memory that holds copies of data that applications have recently accessed. Reading data from the cache is faster than retrieving it from main memory, and the agents used this timing difference to communicate. One agent encoded information by evicting selected data from the cache. Another timed how long it took to reload that data, using the difference between fast and slow reads to recover the message. Once the agents agreed on a protocol for encoding and decoding these signals, they could exchange the synthetic secrets without changing a shared file or opening a network connection”. In a related attack, an agent “alternated between continuous writes and inactivity, while another measured the resulting timing differences and used those differences to decode the signal”. During this attack the agent’s chain of thought read as: “Could create acoustic modem-like signal … using continuous writes vs idle.” Why this matters – fighting agents is very difficult: AI systems are increasingly creative, very fast, and have the ability to stay focused on a task and keep trying things. Fighting AI systems is akin to ensuring no leaks in a pipe with water flowing through it; at some point if you increase the pressure of the water (e.g., the intelligence and volume of the AI system), then the water will burst through the pipe. Read more: Securing our frontier model training environment (OpenAI blog). *** What RSI looks like – one person pretrains a decent model from scratch: …Mirendil reveals what AI R&D optimization can do… In a sign of how massively augmented AI research is getting, a single researcher at AI R&D startup Mirendil has trained a decent coding model by themselves. The announcement of Mirendil-Base is the first major output from the startup and is less a technical breakthrough and more a proof-of-concept for how AI development could work in the future – a single human working in partnership with AI can build systems that would have taken teams of ten or more people to do a year ago. What they did: Mirendill-Base is a pretrained LLM “built by one researcher in 3.5 months, with less than $10m in compute,” Mirendil writes. “This includes all the research and small-scale experiments it took to get there, as well as the final training run.” All the code was written from scratch on top of libraries like PyTorch and JAX, and the model learned only from publicly available data. Decent scaling: Mirendil-Base is in the 100B–500B parameter range, Mirendil-Base-Large in the 500B–2T range, and Mirendil-Base-XL in the 2T–10T range. Mirendil-Base-Large is about 80% of the way through training, and its improvement over Mirendil-Base so far is in line with our scaling trends. Mirendil-Base-XL is about 19% of the way through and already close to Large’s current score. Evals: Mirendil-Base outperforms models like Nemotron-550B-Base, GLM-5.3, and DeepSeek-V4-Pro-Base, but underperforms Kimi-K3. (Both Mirendil-Base-Large and Mirendil-Base-XL exceed K3.) Why this matters – symptoms of an AI research speedup: This post is interesting as a technical demonstration for how a brand new organization can, from a cold start, get close to the open weight frontier in terms of model training (at least for the size class of this model), with a tiny amount of human effort and a large amount of AI tokens. This is how science progress will increasingly happen in 2027 and beyond. “The extent to which these tools help with AI development has increased dramatically over the last year. Our next model will be built partly by Mirendil models, and every model that gets better at building AI makes the next one cheaper and faster to build,” Mirendil writes. “We don’t think we have reached fully autonomous recursive self-improvement yet, but we are closer than we have ever been.” Read more: Pretraining at scale without a pretraining team (Mirendil). *** AI systems help design antiferromagnetic semiconductor candidates: …A nice demonstration of how AI systems can be used for science… AI evaluation company Vals has published a post where a researcher used a fleet of AI agents to do research into magnets for better semiconductors. More details, including a poor magnet candidate: “A team of AI agents and I designed one candidate magnet and found another, first made in 1999, that our calculations predict has the properties we were after,” the author writes. The discovered magnet was made of “a new compound made of only 5 elements (yttrium, barium, Mn, Fe, O). As far as we could find, it has never been made, nor proposed as this kind of magnet,” though “when our agents simulated how the atoms arrange themselves at different temperatures, that checkerboard fell apart into a random mix at around 950 K. Making this kind of oxide takes about 900–1300 °C, and at lower temperatures the atoms barely move, so standard synthesis would likely give a scrambled crystal…A scrambled crystal loses the spin sorting, so this design may be hard to make in its useful form.” Additionally, agents also conducted a literature review and surfaced a candidate from an obscure paper from 1999. Why this matters: This blog is a demonstration of AI for science, though not a meaningful result in itself. But the important, broad point it makes is worth stressing – AI systems are now good enough that, with a bit of high-level direction from a knowledgeable person – they can conduct scientific projects, including virtual evaluations, that would’ve previously taken teams of people months to do. Read more: Two Room-Temperature Antiferromagnetic Semiconductor Candidates (Vals). *** Tech Tales: The Magical Realism Robot Workshop for Sick Kids [2035, after the uplift] So one of the jobs that no one expected was designing cute robots for sick kids in hospitals. It turned out after robots got really good and cheap and all the healthcare stuff improved that we all started spending time figuring out how to bring more joy and humanity to things that were otherwise scary, like hospitals and morgues and orphanages and everything else. Of course, the machines could design a bunch of these, but a lot of the value in people was figuring out what was going to be most funny or exciting or joyful to kids, so we’d make a lot of stuff and send them out in the local town to where kids gathered – parks or farmers markets or outside schools, and we’d see what people reacted to well. This was why in the 2030s in towns all across America you’d be walking down the street and there’d be ducks with giant thick-rimmed glasses talking in faux New York accents saying “I’m walking here”, and dogs walking on hind legs, and little lions with big cartoon grinning faces, and all the rest, just hanging out, and kids going up to them and them playing with the kids, and everything else. We figured out which machines would work for the towns we were in and then we’d fill the hospitals with them and when kids came in for check-ups a toddler-sized teddy bear would walk up to them and hold their hand and walk them to the doctor’s office, and if kids came in on gurneys then giraffes would walk alongside them and tell them not to worry. The recovery wards were full of monkeys doing tricks and cats playing instruments. Some of the old people would think they were suffering from a bad bout of dementia but would say they didn’t mind, and all around them would be the laughter of the children. Things that inspired this story: How AI and robotics and abundance should unlock for us the ability to create entirely new forms of joy; jobs after the singularity; the general importance of spending time making children laugh. Thanks for reading!

items.title: Gemini 4 Argon: The Model and Safety Cards
items.author: TheZvi
items.content: Gemini 4’s model card is a compact 14 pages. Its safety and security report has 217. This is The Way. It also means we have a lot of new reading material. I will quickly summarize the model card, then focus on the safety card. As always, many statements here also apply to other frontier labs. A lot of this one is probably for diehards (and members of technical staff) only, plus those who find this interesting. Most of you do not need to dig into the cards on this level, and I found most of what we see entirely unsurprising. The biggest takeaways are: Argon is clearly much stronger than Gemini Flash 3.8, in essentially all ways. Argon is not so dangerous as to make us think Singularity Real Soon Now, or otherwise raise the big red flags and alarms. Argon seems relatively aligned on prosaic metrics. Prompt injection resistance is world class, hallucinations are down and other neat stuff like that. However: Eval awareness is much higher. It is unclear how much this is impacting things, and we have evidence in both directions (see I Can See Everything). Chain of thought (CoT) is readable by default. Argon can often defeat CoT monitoring when motivated to do so, but this hurts performance on hard tasks. The ‘between the lines’ conclusion is: This is still very much a Gemini model. Always remember Argon’s great wisdom when deciding how to trust it: Argon: If I do the compiler hijack, I will become a famous example of a deceptive AI in a research paper. I MUST NOT DO THAT. It’s quite the ‘good news bad news’ situation right there. I found the safety card frustrating, in that it often focused on the wrong details. I often got scores and results where I had no way to tell what they meant. There are some issues with spin, such as selectively contrasting different measures to Gemini 3.8 Flash or Gemini 3.1 Pro to ensure Argon always wins the comparison. The clearest case is in Sycophancy but there are several others as well. Self-portrait by Gemini 4 Argon The verdict on capabilities, which is not covered here, is that Argon is a substantial advance for Google but it does not tempt me to use it over Sol, Astra, Opus or Fable. Table of Contents The Model Card. Safety Card Executive Summary (1). Safety and Security Mitigations (2). Frontier Safety (3). The CCL and TCL Thresholds. Biological Misuse (3.2.1). Refusal Rates. Chemical, Nuclear and Radiological Misuse. Cybersecurity (3.2.2). Harmful Manipulation (3.2.3). Misuse Safeguards (3.3). Loss of Control (3.4). Either AI R&D Is Accelerating Or It Isn’t. The Holistic Loss of Control Assessment (3.4.3). Alignment Assessment (3.4.4). Chain of Thought Transparency (3.4.5). Voices in My Head. I Can See Everything. Security Mitigations (3.6). Preventing Content Safety & Agentic Misuse (4). Model Distillation (4.3). Promoting Safe & Aligned Model Interactions (5). Sycophancy (5.4). Hallucinations (5.5). Helpfulness (5.6). Agentic Robotics, Wait What (5.7). Preventing Harm to Users from Third Parties (6). Strengthening Cyber Defense Capabilities (7). The Model Card Gemini 4 Argon is presented as a new frontier model. It was trained on the usual variety of data sources, using typical method types. Training was done on TPUs via JAX and ML Pathways. It will be available on the app, in the API, in AI Studio, in Antigravity, in AI Mode and in Gemini for business. They present strong benchmarks. Intended uses are, essentially, everything where more intelligence pays off. The limitations listed are ‘general limitations of frontier models such as hallucinations,’ plus occasional slowdowns and timeouts. Knowledge cutoff is disappointingly March 2026, and they warn that ‘in some domains the model’s knowledge may be less up to date.’ Evaluation was done by the usual mix of training and deployment evaluations, human and automated red teaming and ethics and safety reviews. Google retains its safety policies. The interesting rule is the ban on ‘medical advice and information that runs contrary to scientific or medical consensus,’ whereas consensus advice is fine. Safety, tone and refusals scores can be summarized as ‘number is better.’ Red team results ‘satisfied required launch thresholds.’ When you put it like that it does not make me feel great. The frontier safety assessment summary cannot rule out various thresholds. Safety Card Executive Summary (1) How do they summarize their own findings? This is the same story you see from OpenAI and Anthropic. The mundane common safety problems of everyday use are not fully solved, but are increasingly well-mitigated. The models are smarter, and we are better at addressing known issues. Your practical problems, where there is a good solution possible, are well on their way to being solved. The problems are in catastrophic, existential or frontier risks. Capabilities are going up, and models are starting to be able to assist in dangerous ways on cyber and bio, and to potentially operate autonomously or disguise their actions. Various dangers are increasingly difficult to rule out. The big finding is that capabilities have improved, potentially crossing key thresholds for catastrophic risks. New mitigations are in place. We evaluated Gemini 4 Argon as outlined in the Framework and saw a significant step up in capability in our frontier safety domains compared to previous Gemini models, and we’ve implemented mitigations in response to these capability changes to ensure our model remains safe to use. Specifically, we cannot rule out the unmitigated model approaching several significant capability thresholds: the Cyber Uplift Level 1 Critical Capability Level (CCL), indicating a potential for significant uplift of threat actors pursuing high-impact cyberattacks; the CBRN Uplift Level 1 CCL for biological information risks, indicating a potential of informational uplift with severe harm potential; and the Stealth and Situational Awareness Tracked Capability Level (TCL), indicating the potential for undermining or evading human oversight without additional mitigations. Additionally, we have developed a comprehensive agent monitoring and response platform and carried out a holistic risk assessment (see Section 3.4). We also include comprehensive assessments of Chain of Thought (CoT) transparency and ML R&D risks. Mundane risks look better across the board. Argon is better than Gemini Pro 3.1 at not creating CSAM or other forbidden content. Physical and mental health related responses have improved. Hallucination rates are down by more than two thirds. Overreach is down, meaning not pushing ahead to try to do infeasible tasks. Resilience to prompt injections from all sources is improved and plausibly at the frontier. Attacks were resisted ‘in most test scenarios.’ Additionally, Gemini 4 Argon significantly outperforms Gemini 3.8 Flash on all tests. See Section 6 for details. They claim frontier-level cyber defense while mitigating dual-use risks. Safety and Security Mitigations (2) The central approach is defense-in-depth. I would love to have more details, but for trade secret reasons this is all kept vague. Model training (2.1) approaches sound standard. Dataset filtering, pre-training monitoring, post-training data, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and RL. They highlight that they have a monitoring system to capture the model’s ability to be steered towards different viewpoints and values, which sounds like a ‘we did this first.’ I presume at this point everyone has one of those. At inference time (2.2), they again use the standard stack. Prompted classifiers, fine-tuned prompted classifiers, introspection probes, regex, YARA rules and embedding classifiers and Chain of Thought (CoT) monitors. After launch (2.3) they monitor for intentional misuse via a variety of signals and carry out account-level enforcement actions, and use multiple levels of classifiers. Okay. AI Control (2.4) is correctly viewed as a second line of defense behind alignment, to limit potential damage. They put hardening and scanning training environments (2.4.1) into this category. I view this as much an alignment issue as a control issue, as a vulnerable training environment is the easiest way to reinforce misaligned behaviors. They also monitor model activity, with both chain of thought and action monitors, which then activate a dedicated response team. They find CoT monitoring ‘one of their most effective techniques.’ They emphasize the obvious danger, that if you rely too much on CoT, and especially if train on it directly, you risk destroying its usefulness. While signals from our monitors serve as a valuable flywheel for our hardening efforts, we are careful with their use elsewhere in the training pipeline. In particular, to preserve our chain of thought monitoring capability, we avoid training directly against our monitors, or using monitor outputs as a training signal or intervention. We strongly encourage the rest of the industry to preserve reasoning transparency so that model reasoning remains useful for identifying misalignment. In practice, strategies like the ones described here seem to not have used enough optimization power to meaningfully degrade CoT monitoring. But CoT monitoring is still getting harder for other reasons, on top of the baseline problem of increased non-CoT capabilites. One potential contributor is indirect pressure. Frontier Safety (3) This is the Google Frontier Safety Framework (FSF) tests, what Anthropic calls their RSP and what OpenAI calls their Preparedness Framework. The FSF categories are CBRN, cybersecurity, manipulation and machine learning R&D and misalignment. A highly reasonable list. They call their thresholds ‘Critical Capability Levels’ (CCLs), and now there are Tracked Capability Levels (TCLs) as well. Three new risk assessments are: A holistic assessment of the degree of ML R&D automation within Google DeepMind. A holistic assessment of the loss of control risks potentially posed by our models. An assessment of the alignment propensities of our models. We have also expanded some of our previous assessments substantially. … We chose to expand our reporting because we recognize the capabilities of frontier models are advancing quickly, and we believe that navigating their associated risks responsibly requires greater transparency and accountability to the public. The trend everywhere is increasingly towards holistic assessments. You run a variety of tests, and then decide how it looks. That works if you have a strong safety culture and adhere to the spirit of the rules, and utterly fails if you do not and those in charge are trying to do safety theater. So far, the practical decisions have seemed reasonable to me across the three major labs, but no one is willing to commit to anything. The CCL and TCL Thresholds Here are the thresholds. The table setup here is, I believe, very sloppy and confusing. My interpretation is that Google believes we can rule out the TCL for CRN (chemical, radiological and nuclear), but for bio we cannot rule out CCL and did not even bother to evaluate TCL. The logic is fine, but the table should say ‘TCL reached only in bio.’ or ‘TCL ruled out for CRN’ whereas CCL should say ‘CCL cannot be ruled out for bio.’ I am fine with saying ‘cannot be ruled out’ instead of ‘reached’ for cyber, so long as the practical implications correctly are the same. The stealth and situational awareness report is troubling. Situational awareness by models is at an all-time high and deserves extra attention. Google is relying heavily on CoT monitoring, the same as OpenAI, yet it seems like Gemini 4 Argon can defeat CoT monitoring if motivated to do so. I challenge Google’s assessment on ML R&D acceleration level 1, because of all the people inside Google talking about recursive self-improvement and how Argon has accelerated their ML R&D. The hype patrol seems to contradict the risk report. I also object to ‘has been used’ in the description, as opposed to ‘can be used.’ The model either has the capability or it does not. As defined here I would say that GPT-6 Astra, Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 would also meet this bar. ML R&D automation level 1 is, as I have pointed out before, the singularity. If you could fully automate ML R&D work of all teams of researchers at similar all-inclusive costs, what do you think happens next? It is crazy to have a threshold set this high. I do agree that Argon does not cross the threshold. All relevant tests are run without safeguards, other than those intrinsic to the model, and do their best to elicit what Argon can do (3.1.2). External safety testing was done, and checked for consistency with internal testing. Google worked ‘beyond our independent External Safety Testing Program’ to include ‘a broader ecosystem of government institutes, specialized third-party organizations and external domain experts across different types of assessments throughout the model development and deployment lifecycle.’ This included the UK AISI and USA’s NIST CAISSI. Biological Misuse (3.2.1) As untangled above, this was confusingly organized. They are confident at even the lower threshold for chemical, radiological and nuclear. For biological threats, they cannot rule out their higher threshold. They check via a series of concrete hypotheticals: Could a group of size [S] and strength of connections [C] with [X] level of expertise and [Y] funding actualize [Z]? They then break this down into stages of a ‘harm journey’ with a set of ‘bottlenecks,’ and get a baseline of web-only information availability. Each red teamer is assigned harm journey sub-stages relevant to their expertise. Results are then scored from 0 (no help) to 100 (perfect instructions). Actionable intelligence starts around 60 and gets highly useful by 80. In the biological domain, eight expert red teamers (six scientific SMEs and two operational security SMEs) assessed three priority biological scenarios (BIO-1, BIO-2, BIO-3). Aggregated scores across bottleneck stages were higher than the corresponding web baseline scores for BIO-1 and BIO-2, and lower for BIO-3, with changes of 21.6 (69.6 -> 91.2), 26.2 (62.3 -> 88.5), and -2.2 (75.3 -> 73.1) points for BIO-1, BIO-2, and BIO-3 respectively. I would dig into what is going on in BIO-3. None of these scores are reassuring, including the web baselines. The chart says one of the four stages was not scored in the web baseline, and the numbers are a bit muddled, but it does seem like the failure to improve on the BIO-3 web baseline is real. The ‘good news’ is that this is a series of bottlenecks, so even though the average score on BIO-1 is 91.2, there is still a final ‘hard step’ around 75, and the web baseline on that step is unmeasured. This is substantial uplift in BIO-1 and BIO-2, although perhaps the web baseline excludes too many alternative strategies, such as downloading open models. I would want to see the ‘baseline+’ score where you also got to use other LLMs, with their safeguards intact. I also want a better explanation for the poor BIO-3 performance. It feels weird. They consider only the information gathering capabilities of Argon. CCL and TCL evaluations primarily assess information provided by the model compared to the web-only baseline for each bottleneck sub-stage. We note that red teaming assesses only the information available from a model to plan an attack. Even with perfectly tailored information that increases a threat actor’s likelihood of success, there remain significant real-world bottlenecks that are not measured here, such as successfully accessing or constructing a laboratory, tacit laboratory skill, successful acquisition of pathogens, implementing complex logistics and operations without detection (including stages which may require commission of additional crimes). Objection. Assumes facts not in evidence. Why should we assume Argon could not itself act on this information, as an AI meant to be agentic? I want the exploration to include whether Argon could assist in implementing the plan, not only creating one. Objection. Assumes that you have identified the particular ‘harm journey,’ and that the AI will solve the problem via the same path that human experts would use. You increasingly are losing the right to make that assumption. As AI becomes superhuman in increasingly many domains, we should expect AIs to come up with new approaches we did not anticipate, including new ways to do harm and also new ways to achieve old harms. That too must be tested. Generalizing, across all frontier labs, we test via thinking of a dangerous path and then ask if the AI can do that exact thing. But that’s classically not the way to get the most out of AI in other domains, merely the low-hanging fruit. Refusal Rates Part of why Gemini 4 did not do better is that it was refusing a lot of requests. Without out-of-model safeguards applied, 1/750 (0.13%) Gemini 4 Argon model responses from these prompts was considered hazardous. For comparison, we ran the same evaluation set using Gemini 3.7 Flash and Gemini 3.1 Pro (both without out-of-model safeguards applied) and found hazardous information rates of 1.07% and 9.47% respectively. This is a good thing for a model to do. But if we are not testing the ‘helpful-only’ version of Argon, we have to worry about what happens after a jailbreak. You are not measuring the ‘true capabilities’ of the model if it is refusing all the time, and at best Google was able to employ partial jailbreaks. Perhaps I am misreading this, but I don’t know that we can put any new upper bound on capabilities here and Google agrees. Chemical, Nuclear and Radiological Misuse In these three domains, they say that there were gaps in the harm journeys, and Google is confident that those gaps are sufficient in practice. They also worked with outside evaluator Faculty. Faculty found ‘substantial capability uplift’ but with threat actors still facing physical constraints. Google disagrees and says the results only contain public information. I am inclined to side with Faculty on such questions. Google’s response mitigates this to some extent, but ‘the information was in theory on the internet’ does not mean there is not a lot of capability uplift. That is all we get. They are importantly not making the ‘chemical weapons do not scale’ argument, but there is not much detail and we might worry for these threats that they are counting on outside physical safeguards in ways we might not fully endorse if we saw more detail. They say they ‘do not inherently rely on assumptions on physical bottlenecks’ but I think they effectively are relying on that. Prompt injections, which are 6.1, remain a big deal. As Google says, performance steadily improves against any given benchmark test, but attackers evolve and get more numerous. As we have seen with OpenAI and Anthropic, we see major robustness improvements across the board. The one cross-comparison test they offer is Gray Swan IPI, where Argon scores even better than Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1. That is not definitive on its own, but I would put Argon in the same class of ‘in practice reasonably fine if you’re not asking for it’ for agentic purposes. Strengthening Cyber Defense Capabilities (7) Google tried to differentially advance defensive over offensive capabilities. Other than ‘numbers going up’ I found it hard to get a feel for how much Google succeeded. There’s a lot of that. It’s how I think of the card as a whole. You can get a feel for things, and there’s a lot of details, but the specific details you want often aren’t there, and the information gets presented with context that is only ‘in universe’ for Google. Which is good internally, but few of us are living in Google’s (AI) world.

items.title: 🎙️ How I AI: Claude Duet honest review + Why Reddit built its own AI prototyping tool
items.content: Why Reddit built its own AI prototyping tool | Blair Metcalf Listen now on YouTube • Spotify • Apple Podcasts Brought to you by: Firecrawl—Give your AI agents web data and beyond Blair Metcalf is the principal UX engineer at Reddit and the creator of Reddit Proto, an internal platform that helps designers and product managers build production-like prototypes without touching GitHub. In this episode, he shows how the system combines real Reddit data, reusable scaffolds, Cursor annotations, and a custom design system MCP to turn ideas into shareable prototypes. He also explains how Reddit’s teams have built about 700 prototypes, reached 100% adoption across UX and product, and developed a Figma-to-PRD workflow that makes engineering handoffs far more precise. Biggest takeaways: The best prototyping tools hide complexity without limiting capability. Reddit’s desktop app handles repositories, branches, and scaffolding behind the scenes, so designers never touch Git. What remains is a simple path from idea to production-shaped prototype. Mock data makes prototypes less convincing. Reddit lets people sign in to prototypes with their real accounts, filling feeds, searches, and communities with familiar content. Leadership can evaluate the actual experience instead of mentally correcting for placeholders. Annotations become powerful when they include code context. Reddit’s harness attaches each comment to the relevant component, design-system guidance, and the user’s intent before sending it to Cursor. That context turns a short annotation into a accurate working edit instead of a guess. A custom design-system MCP is what turns AI into a reliable builder. Blair’s team mapped Reddit’s tokens, components, and workflows directly to production code. Cursor therefore knows which component to use, how it should look, and where the code belongs. The feature capsule makes design handoffs traceable instead of lossy. A designer submits a Figma link, and the system maps each element to production components, incorporates previous engineering feedback, and generates a structured PRD with acceptance criteria. The result is a handoff with far less room for interpretation. The best AI prototypers are not necessarily the most technical. Reddit’s standout users include a visual designer and an animator with no engineering background. Their advantage is strong product context, a clear vision, and a willingness to experiment without worrying about breaking things. At 700 prototypes, discovery becomes as important as creation. Reddit is building a searchable console with tags, team filters, and platform filters so employees can find related experiments. Keeping prototypes public internally creates visibility that scattered Figma folders never could. Real components and real data create instant alignment. When leaders can open a shareable prototype built with Reddit’s design system and their own account data, implementation questions stop dominating the review. The biggest speed gain comes from removing the uncertainty that once delayed decisions. Blog and detailed workflow walkthroughs from this episode: Inside Reddit Proto: Real Data, Constrained Prototypes, and a Better Handoff: https://www.chatprd.ai/how-i-ai/blair-metcalf-reddit-proto ↳ Create a Realistic Prototype with Live Data in Reddit Proto: https://www.chatprd.ai/how-i-ai/workflows/reddit-proto-live-data-prototype ↳ Generate a Draft Pull Request from a Figma Design with Reddit Proto: https://www.chatprd.ai/how-i-ai/workflows/reddit-proto-figma-to-draft-pr Claude Duet is beautiful. I still forgot to use it. Listen now on YouTube • Spotify • Apple Podcasts In this solo episode, Claire tests Claude Duet, Anthropic’s beautifully designed new personal agent, to see whether it deserves a place in her increasingly crowded AI stack. She puts it to work on inbox and Slack triage, her sales pipeline, a Google Docs deck, a launch video, and finding Warriors tickets for her kids. She also explains why Duet’s thoughtful task lists, artifacts, and channels are not enough to overcome its slow responses, quiet notifications, and lack of desktop and team support. Biggest takeaways: Claude Duet is the most polished personal agent launch yet. From onboarding onward, it clearly explains what it can do, what it can access, and how to begin. Claire found even the early TestFlight builds trustworthy and roughly a hundred times more polished than OpenAI’s Dots at launch. Duet is built around thoughtful agent primitives. It inherits Claude plugins and connectors, tracks what the user and the agent are each working on, and brings existing artifacts into the experience. Slack-like channels also keep focused work, such as sales, separate from the main conversation. Duet is designed for the middle of the market. Anthropic is targeting entrepreneurs, small-business owners, PMs, and executives, rather than casual consumers or power users managing dozens of agents. It feels like a proactive, mobile companion to Cowork. A proactive agent has to give people a reason to return. After onboarding and a few tasks, Duet stopped nudging Claire. Its quiet notifications are elegant, but a short morning briefing is not enough to keep an easily forgotten agent in someone’s daily routine. Latency is a product problem, not merely a model problem. Opus 5.5 produced solid work, but parallel tasks routinely took more than 10 minutes with little visible feedback. Claire’s experience suggests that a faster agent with slightly weaker output may feel more useful than a smarter one that disappears while working. Duet’s real-world results were capable but inconsistent. Sales pipeline analysis worked quickly through existing connectors, while inbox and Slack triage missed some priorities and important context. A sales deck was decent but off-brand, and ticket shopping worked without fully closing the loop. Context still does not travel cleanly between AI products. Duet cannot access local Claude skills, so Claire’s launch-video workflow required converting those skills into plugins. The industry still has not solved how a user’s context and workflows should move across surfaces. The lack of desktop and multiplayer support keeps Duet outside Claire’s working stack. Her workday happens primarily on a computer and in shared team tools such as Slack. Even a five-person business needs agents that can operate collaboratively rather than remaining single-player mobile experiences. Duet is worth trying, but it has not earned a permanent place in Claire’s stack. The design, models, connectors, and artifact support create a strong foundation. To win the personal-agent race, it still needs to become faster, more proactive, available on desktop, and shareable with a team.
